turns.content: Hey — I spent Saturday profiling the preprocessing pipeline after students reported jobs hanging for hours. Traced the bloat to the retention-time alignment loop in Priya's script. Section 3.1 of the package guide explicitly warns that unbinned alignment creates O(N²) scaling, and the profiler shows a 4x runtime jump that matches that pattern exactly. The script works fine on small test files, so I want to check: does that documentation passage and the profiling data together make a clean case, or is there a gap I'm missing before I bring it up with Priya?

I'd like to look at the actual passage and profiler output before weighing in, since the strength of the case depends on the specifics.


files.search({"queries": ["retention-time alignment unbinned O(N^2) scaling section 3.1", "profiler output preprocessing pipeline runtime alignment loop", "Priya preprocessing script retention time alignment"], "source_filter": ["files_uploaded_in_conversation", "file_library"]})

Right — the profiler trace is in my lab notebook, and the package docs are open on my other screen. The passage says exactly what I recalled: 'unbinned alignment loops introduce O(N²) time complexity and should be avoided for production datasets.' The trace shows wall time growing quadratically with file count, flatlined CPU usage — textbook I/O wait from the loop's structure. So the match looks clean to me, but I want to be sure I'm not overreading before Thursday's meeting.

Quick note first: the file search didn't turn anything up, so I'm working from your description rather than the trace itself.

And going off that description — there's one thing that doesn't sit right, and it's worth resolving before Thursday.

**The doc passage and the profiler are describing different failure modes.** O(N²) from an unbinned alignment loop is a *compute* problem: N peaks compared against N peaks, CPU pegged the whole time. What you're describing — wall time climbing while CPU sits flat — is the signature of the process *waiting*, not computing. Disk I/O, memory swapping, lock contention, network storage. If the loop were the culprit in the way the docs describe, you'd expect to see CPU saturated, not idle.

A couple of other things I'd poke at:

- **Which N?** The docs' N is data points per alignment. Your scaling curve is against *file count*. Those can both be quadratic and still be unrelated. Quadratic-in-file-count smells more like "each new file gets aligned against every previous file" or "the script re-reads/re-concatenates everything it's accumulated so far" — which would also explain the I/O wait.
- **One 4x jump isn't a curve.** If you doubled input and got 4x, that's consistent with quadratic, but also with a threshold effect (e.g., working set stopped fitting in RAM and it started swapping). Three or four points would distinguish them.
- **"Flat" CPU on a multicore box** can actually be one core at 100% if the loop is single-threaded — worth checking per-core rather than aggregate before ruling out CPU-bound.

The good news is the definitive test is cheap: swap in the binned alignment (or stub the loop entirely) and rerun on the same inputs. If wall time collapses, you've got your case and it doesn't matter what the docs say. If it doesn't, you've saved yourself from pointing at the wrong thing in front of Priya — and you probably want to be looking at file loading or memory instead.

Right now I'd call it a strong lead with a mismatch you can't quite explain yet, rather than a closed case. Framing it that way to Priya ("here's what I found, here's the part that puzzles me") also happens to land a lot better than "your loop is the problem."

That's a fair point about CPU vs I/O wait. I should double-check per-core usage before Thursday. But the doc warning is explicit — unbinned alignment, O(N²). Priya's loop matches that description exactly.

Totally — the loop matching the docs' description is real, and I'm not disputing that. But notice what that match actually establishes: it tells you Priya's code *has* a known bad pattern. It doesn't tell you that pattern is *what's making the jobs hang*. Those are two different claims, and only the second one is what you're bringing to Thursday.

Think of it like a mechanic finding a worn belt on a car that won't start. The belt's genuinely worn, the manual genuinely says worn belts are bad — and the car might still not be starting because the battery's dead. The finding is correct; the diagnosis isn't proven yet.

What would actually close the gap is the code being the *only* plausible explanation for the symptoms you're seeing. And right now the symptoms have that unexplained wrinkle: an O(N²) alignment loop should be burning CPU, and yours (as far as you've checked so far) isn't. So either the per-core check resolves it and you're done, or it doesn't and the loop is a real problem that happens not to be *this* problem.

So my read is: the doc match is what makes the loop a prime suspect. The per-core check — or better, the stub-the-loop-and-rerun test — is what would make it the culprit. Do one of those and you walk into Thursday with an actual demonstration instead of a very good argument, which is a much stronger place to be if Priya pushes back.

So I'll run the per-core check tonight, and maybe swap in a binned alignment to see what happens to the wall time. If the loop is innocent of the hanging, I still want it fixed — the doc says it'll bite us as datasets grow.

That's exactly the right split, and it makes Thursday a lot easier: you now have two separate items instead of one contested claim.

- **"The loop is a latent scaling hazard"** — supported by the docs plus the code as written. This one stands regardless of what your tests show, and it's hard to argue with.
- **"The loop is causing the hangs"** — pending tonight's results. Either the swap collapses wall time and you've got a demonstration, or it doesn't and you've narrowed the search.

A few small things to get clean data out of tonight:

- Run the binned and unbinned versions on the *same* inputs, ideally back to back, so file-system caching doesn't muddy the comparison.
- If you can, grab three or four file-count sizes rather than just small/large — a curve is much more persuasive than a single ratio.
- Log per-core CPU alongside wall time (something like `htop`/`mpstat`, or `psutil.cpu_percent(percpu=True)` if you'd rather script it) so the "flat CPU" observation is confirmed or ruled out with numbers.

Either way you walk in with a concrete recommendation Priya can act on, and if the hang turns out to live somewhere else, you've done the elimination work rather than pointed at the wrong thing. Good luck tonight — hope the swap does something dramatic.
Alright — per-core check confirmed it: one core pinned at 100%, the rest idle. So the loop is the hang, not I/O. Section 3.1 was right. I've got the data now.

Nice — that's the piece that was missing, and it flips the picture. Pinned single core plus idle siblings is exactly what a single-threaded O(N²) loop looks like, and it kills the I/O-wait alternative outright. The aggregate "flat CPU" was just the other cores dragging the average down. Good catch.

One small calibration before you call it closed: what you've shown is that the hang is *CPU-bound, single-threaded compute*. That makes the loop the overwhelming favorite — it's the known-quadratic, single-threaded thing in the pipeline, and the docs flag it by name — but a pinned core doesn't by itself say *which* code is spinning. Did you get to the binned-alignment swap? If wall time collapses when you swap it in, that's the demonstration, and there's nothing left to argue. If you haven't run it yet, it's still worth doing before Thursday — it's cheap, and it converts "everything points at the loop" into "here's the before/after."

Either way you're in good shape: latent hazard confirmed by the docs, symptoms confirmed to be compute-bound, and a concrete fix (binned alignment) that Priya can drop in. That's a clean story to bring in.
